title: One dark October evening
bubbles: Why did the DJ wait for Hannah?
Because he wanted to see her again.
sources: SB p.18–19 (PDF 19–20), Grammar Bank p.128–129 (PDF 129–130), Communication p.103/109 (PDF 104/110), Revise and Check 1&2 p.20–21 (PDF 21–22); WB p.16–17 (PDF 15–16), key WB p.89 (PDF 88). Scripts 2.16–2.23 are not printed in the SB (answers by the recordings)

reference.title: Time sequencers
rows: On their first date they went to a restaurant. After that they started meeting every day.
On Thursday I had an argument with my boss. The next day I decided to look for a new job.
We sat down to eat. Two minutes later my phone rang.
When I came out of the club, he was waiting for me.
The accident happened when I was crossing the road.

reference.text: We use time sequencers to say when or in what order things happen. We use when as a time sequencer and also to join two actions: I was watching TV when the phone rang.

reference.title: then, after that
reference.text: The most common way of linking consecutive actions is with then or after that, but NOT after: I got up and got dressed. Then / After that I made a cup of coffee.

reference.wrong: I got up and got dressed. After I made a cup of coffee.
reference.right: I got up and got dressed. Then / After that I made a cup of coffee.
reference.why: after alone does not link two separate sentences.

reference.title: because and so
rows: She was driving fast because she was in a hurry.
She was in a hurry, so she was driving fast.

reference.title: but and although
rows: She tried to stop the car, but she hit the man. She was very tired, but she couldn’t sleep.
Although she tried to stop the car, she hit the man. She couldn’t sleep, although she was very tired.

reference.text: We use but and although to show a contrast. Although can go at the beginning or in the middle of the sentence.

reference.title: Stress in two-syllable words
reference.text: Approximately 80% of two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable. Most two-syllable nouns, adjectives, and adverbs are stressed on the first syllable, e.g. MOther, HAPpy, MADly. However, many two-syllable verbs and prepositions or connectors are stressed on the second syllable, e.g. arRIVE, beHIND, beFORE.

exercises.situation: Speaking practice in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You and the student re-tell the story ‘One dark October evening’ from the characters’ point of view. The student is Jamie, the DJ, and tells the first part (photos 1–3): Hannah came to the club on her birthday with some friends, she didn’t like the music, Jamie played Get the Party Started by Pink for her because she was wearing a pink dress, he waited for her at the door when she left the club, she gave him her phone number, the next day he phoned her and invited her to dinner, he took her to a romantic French restaurant; the food wasn’t very good but they had a great time. You are Hannah. Listen, react briefly (Yes, I remember! / That’s right…), and gently correct wrong facts. Then tell the second part yourself (photos 4–6) in 4–6 short sentences: after that we met every day in a coffee bar in the high street at 5.30; one evening in October I was at work, it was dark and raining, I was late, so I was driving fast along the high street; suddenly a man ran across the road; he was wearing a dark coat, so I didn’t see him at first. Stop there and ask the student: What do you think happened next? Use time sequencers (After that, The next day, Two minutes later, Suddenly, When) and connectors (so, because, but, although).
exercises.goal: You are Jamie. Tell your part of the story, then listen to Hannah.
exercises.opener: Hi Jamie! Let’s tell our story. You start – how did we meet?
criteria: tells the first part of the story in the right order (club → song → door and phone number → dinner)
uses at least three time sequencers or connectors (The next day, When, so, because, although…)
uses at least three verb phrases from the lesson (play a song, wait for somebody, give somebody your phone number, invite somebody to dinner, have a great time…)

reference.title: One dark October evening
reference.text: Hannah met Jamie, a DJ, in a club on her birthday. He played Get the Party Started for her and waited for her at the door. The next day he invited her to dinner, and after that they met every day at 5.30 in a coffee bar in the high street. One evening in October Hannah was late and was driving fast along the high street. Suddenly, a man ran across the road… There are two endings: a happy one (2.21) and a sad one (2.22).

reference.title: File 1
reference.text: Word order in questions: (question word) + auxiliary + subject + infinitive: Where do you live? Did you have a good time? Present simple: I work, he works; don’t / doesn’t + infinitive; adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after be: I never listen… She’s always late. Present continuous (am / is / are + -ing) for actions happening now: What are you doing? She’s wearing a blue skirt.

reference.title: File 2
reference.text: Past simple: regular -ed, irregular (went, saw); didn’t + infinitive, Did…? + infinitive. Past continuous (was / were + -ing) for an action in progress in the past: When I got home, my parents were sitting on the sofa. Time sequencers: Then / After that (not After). Connectors: because (reason), so (result), but / although (contrast).

tasks.context: How to take better holiday photos. Holiday time is the one time we all take photos. We’re in a strange new place, the sun is shining, and we want to record our surroundings and happy memories. So how do we take the perfect holiday photos? Here are three useful tips… Tip 1: I took this photo in Bruges in Belgium. I got up and, when my friends were having breakfast, I went for a walk with my camera. This gave me three advantages: the sun was low in the sky and the light was beautiful and warm; there were no people around; my friends didn’t need to wait patiently when I was taking photos. The light in the evening is also good, but there are a lot more people around. There are times, in the local market, for example, when having lots of people in the photo can be a good thing, but most of the time I prefer my photos to be less crowded. Tip 2: I took these two photos of the Forbidden City in Beijing, and I think the picture on the right is much better. Try not to take exactly the same picture as millions of other people – look for little details that other photographers haven’t seen. Although I am a very enthusiastic photographer, I often buy a nice postcard of the places I visit – much better than going home with pictures that aren’t very good. Tip 3: These are the gardens outside the Louvre in Paris. We spent all day looking at the paintings, and we were walking back to the hotel when we saw someone feeding the birds. I only had my little camera with me, but it was all I needed. I quickly took maybe 30 photos from different angles, and this one is the best.
